explanations.answer: Do you not understand what the law says
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul asks, "Tell me, you who want to be under the law, do you not understand what the law says?" (Galatians 4:21). I think it stings a little, because he's asking about the very thing they say they want. And he's about to show them what it says, so stick with me.

explanations.answer: Have you kept every part of the law
explanations.explanation: Good guess, because it sounds like a question a teacher would ask. But Paul doesn't ask whether they've kept the law. He asks, "…do you not understand what the law says?" (Galatians 4:21). He's checking what they've heard, not counting their score. I've been counting cookies for years and I still lose track, so I'm glad that's not the question.

explanations.answer: Who was the first to teach you the law
explanations.explanation: Nice try, baker, but Paul doesn't ask who taught them. He asks, "Tell me, you who want to be under the law, do you not understand what the law says?" (Galatians 4:21). The question is about what the law says, not who said it first. Keep your eyes on the words, and you'll catch these every time.

Close, but Paul says the opposite. He writes that Abraham "had two sons, one by the slave woman and the other by the free woman." (Galatians 4:22). So one mother was a slave woman and the other was a free woman. Two sons, two different mothers, and that difference is the whole lesson.

That's right, baker. Paul says Abraham "had two sons, one by the slave woman and the other by the free woman." (Galatians 4:22). So only one son was born to a free woman. The other mother was a slave woman, and Paul builds the whole lesson on that split.

Yes, baker. Paul says the son by the slave woman "was born according to the flesh" (Galatians 4:23). That's the first blank, and it's the one that sets this son apart from his brother. Two sons, and the first one's birth is described with that word.
Right on, baker. The son by the free woman "was born through the promise" (Galatians 4:23). That's the second blank. Paul puts the word promise on that son, and he'll keep coming back to it.

Harvest sounds like a good word, baker, but it's not in this verse. Paul says one son was born "according to the flesh" and the other "through the promise" (Galatians 4:23). Nothing about crops anywhere. I wish it were, because I'd have a few jokes ready.

Prophets is a fair guess, since Paul does bring in a prophet later. But in this verse, the sons are born "according to the flesh" and "through the promise" (Galatians 4:23). The prophets aren't part of how either son was born. The words you need are flesh and promise.

Temple is a good Bible word, baker, but it doesn't fit here. Paul says the first son was born "according to the flesh" and the second "through the promise" (Galatians 4:23). The blanks are about how each son was born, not about a building. It's flesh and promise this time.

That's it, baker. Paul says, "One covenant is from Mount Sinai and bears children into slavery" (Galatians 4:24). Sinai is the mountain this covenant comes from. Hold onto that name, because Paul ties it to a woman in the very next breath.

Zion is a famous mountain, so I see why it came to mind. But Paul says the covenant that bears children into slavery is "from Mount Sinai" (Galatians 4:24). Zion isn't named in this passage at all. Sinai is the one to remember.

Carmel is a real mountain in the Bible, baker, but Paul doesn't mention it here. He says, "One covenant is from Mount Sinai and bears children into slavery" (Galatians 4:24). The covenant he's talking about comes from Sinai. Carmel just wandered into the answer list.

Yes, baker. Paul says the covenant from Mount Sinai that bears children into slavery: "This is Hagar." (Galatians 4:24). Hagar is the slave woman from Abraham's story. Paul uses her as a picture of that covenant.

Sarah is in the story, but she's the other woman. Paul names the Sinai covenant, the one that bears children into slavery, and says, "This is Hagar." (Galatians 4:24). Sarah is the free woman. Easy to flip them, so don't be hard on yourself.

Rebekah isn't in this passage, baker. Paul says the covenant from Mount Sinai "bears children into slavery: This is Hagar." (Galatians 4:24). Both women he's talking about are in Abraham's household, and that's where you'll find the answer. Rebekah comes along in a later chapter of that family's story.

explanations.answer: She is in slavery with her children
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. Paul says Hagar corresponds to the present-day Jerusalem "because she is in slavery with her children." (Galatians 4:25). The match is about slavery. Nothing else about the city is part of his reason.

explanations.answer: She was buried outside its walls
explanations.explanation: That's a creative answer, but Paul says nothing about where Hagar was buried. His reason is that she "is in slavery with her children." (Galatians 4:25). That's what links her to the present-day Jerusalem. I'd skip the burial plot and stick with the text.

explanations.answer: She once lived inside its gates
explanations.explanation: Reasonable guess, baker, but Paul never says Hagar lived in Jerusalem. He says she corresponds to the present-day Jerusalem "because she is in slavery with her children." (Galatians 4:25). The link is slavery, not an address.

Not quite, baker, and this one matters. Paul says, "But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother." (Galatians 4:26). So the Jerusalem above is free, not in slavery. The slavery belongs to the present-day Jerusalem.

That's right, baker. Paul says, "But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother." (Galatians 4:26). Free, not in slavery. That little word "But" shows he's pointing to a different Jerusalem than the one he just talked about.

explanations.answer: She will have more children than the married woman
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The words say, "…more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband." (Galatians 4:27). That's the reason she gets to rejoice. She starts with none, and the promise is that she ends up with more.

explanations.answer: Her husband will soon come home to her
explanations.explanation: That's a sweet guess, but it's not in these words. The reason given is, "…more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband." (Galatians 4:27). Nothing about a husband coming home. It's all about her children.

explanations.answer: Her fields will soon grow fruitful again
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, baker, but fields never come up. The quote says, "…more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband." (Galatians 4:27). Her reason to rejoice is children, not a harvest.
Yes, baker. Paul says, "Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise." (Galatians 4:28). Isaac was the son born through the promise. Paul puts the Galatian believers right alongside him.

Close family, wrong brother. Paul says, "Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise." (Galatians 4:28). Ishmael is the son of the slave woman, and Paul doesn't name him in this passage. The promise belongs to Isaac.

Esau is a Bible name, baker, but he's a generation later and not in this passage. Paul says, "Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise." (Galatians 4:28). Isaac is the one he compares them to. Esau was Isaac's son, so you're in the right family, just one step too far down.

That's right, baker. Paul says, "At that time, however, the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit." (Galatians 4:29). He doesn't say how or give details here. He just states that it happened.

That would be a nicer story, baker, but it isn't what Paul says. He writes that "the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit." (Galatians 4:29). Persecuted is the word. I'd have liked the cozy version too.

Ignoring is a quieter thing than what Paul describes. He says, "…the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit." (Galatians 4:29). The word is persecuted. That's more than leaving someone alone.

Not this time, baker. Paul says the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit, and then adds, "It is the same now." (Galatians 4:29). So it didn't stay in the past. He says it's still going on.

That's right, baker. After saying the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit, Paul adds, "It is the same now." (Galatians 4:29). So the trouble didn't stay in the past. Paul says it carries on in his own day.

explanations.answer: Her son will never share in the inheritance
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The Scripture says, "…the slave woman's son will never share in the inheritance with the free woman's son." (Galatians 4:30). That's the reason given. It's about the inheritance, and nothing else is added.

explanations.answer: Her son had chosen to live far away
explanations.explanation: That's a thoughtful guess, but the Scripture gives a different reason. It says, "…the slave woman's son will never share in the inheritance with the free woman's son." (Galatians 4:30). There's no mention of him choosing anything. The reason is the inheritance.

explanations.answer: Her son was old enough to live on his own
explanations.explanation: I can see why that came to mind, baker, but it's not the reason in the text. The Scripture says, "…the slave woman's son will never share in the inheritance with the free woman's son." (Galatians 4:30). Age never comes up. It's the inheritance that decides it.

Whoa, baker, Paul says the exact opposite. He ends with, "Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman, but of the free woman." (Galatians 4:31). So no, they are not children of the slave woman. That's the big finish.

That's right, baker. Paul closes with, "Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman, but of the free woman." (Galatians 4:31). So they are children of the free woman, not the slave woman. That's how the passage ends.
